n: The prophecy against Gog continues, repeating the Lord’s declaration of opposition before describing Gog’s defeat in detail.

f.w: I am against thee, O Gog

n: God leads Gog to the mountains of Israel—and to his ruin. The KJV’s “leave but the sixth part” is uncertain; many translations read “drive you along” or “lead you on.”

f.w: leave but the sixth part of thee
f.g: The Hebrew is obscure; it may mean “lead thee on” rather than a fraction of survivors.

n: An archer holds the bow in the left hand and arrows in the right. God knocks both away, leaving the mighty army defenseless.
Gog’s armies die on the very mountains they came to plunder, their bodies left for scavenging birds and beasts—the ultimate disgrace in the ancient world.
Gog will not even reach a city; he falls in the open countryside. God’s word guarantees the outcome.
Judgment reaches beyond the battlefield to Gog’s homeland and to distant coastlands that felt secure. “Carelessly” means in false security.

f.g: Live with a false sense of safety.

n: Through these events God’s holy name will be honored rather than mocked. He calls Himself “the Holy One in Israel,” recalling Isaiah’s favorite title.
So certain is the prophecy that God speaks of it as already finished.

f.w: it is come, and it is done

n: The enemy’s weapons become firewood—enough to burn for seven years. Seven signals completeness; the war is over for good.
Israel won’t need to cut trees for fuel. The plunderers are plundered—a complete reversal of fortunes.

f.w: they shall spoil those that spoiled them

n: Gog receives a mass grave in a valley east of the sea (probably the Dead Sea). The valley is renamed Hamon-gog, “the multitude of Gog.” The stench blocks travelers’ way.

f.g: “Valley of the travelers”—a route used by those passing through.

n: Burying the dead takes seven months. Under the Law of Moses, dead bodies made the land unclean, so burial is an act of purification.

f.w: that they may cleanse the land

n: The whole population joins in, and the day becomes a memorable honor for Israel because God is glorified.
A full-time crew is appointed to search the land and find remaining remains after the seven months.

f.g: Men assigned permanently to the task.

n: Anyone who sees a bone marks it so the burial crew can collect it—showing how thoroughly the land must be cleansed.
A nearby town will be named Hamonah, “multitude,” as a memorial of the event.
The scene shifts to grim symbolism: birds and beasts are invited to a “sacrifice” feast. In this reversal, the enemies of God become the offering.
The mighty warriors and princes are compared to fattened sacrificial animals. Bashan, east of the Jordan, was famous for its well-fed livestock.
In real sacrifice, fat and blood belonged to God alone. Here the image is reversed to show the totality of judgment on the proud.
God’s “table” is set with the horses, chariots, and warriors of a defeated army—the end of human military pride.
All nations will see God’s glory revealed in His judgments. His “hand” represents His power at work.
From that day on, Israel will know the Lord as their God. Deliverance produces lasting recognition.
Now the nations will understand that Israel’s exile was not because their God was weak, but because Israel sinned. God “hid His face”—withdrew His protection—so they fell.

f.w: hid I my face from them

n: Israel’s punishment matched their deeds. God’s justice was fair and measured.
“Now” marks the turn from judgment to mercy. God will restore Jacob’s fortunes and show compassion to the whole house of Israel.

f.w: bring again the captivity of Jacob
f.g: Restore Jacob’s fortunes; bring the captives home.

n: Once restored and safe, Israel will feel the shame of past unfaithfulness—not as condemnation, but as humble remembrance that leads to gratitude.
God’s gathering of Israel from enemy lands will display His holiness before many nations.

f.w: gathered them out of their enemies' lands

n: The same God who sent them into exile brings them all home—leaving no one behind. Both discipline and deliverance come from His hand.

f.w: have left none of them any more there

n: The section on Gog ends with a promise: God will never again hide His face, because He has poured out His Spirit on Israel. This bridges into Ezekiel’s great temple vision that follows.

f.w: I have poured out my spirit
